title: Original: The Night Patrol
passage:
The Night Patrol

Every evening, just after the last beachgoer packs up an umbrella and the light turns the colour of weak tea, a small group gathers at the edge of Corrimal Beach. They carry clipboards, torches wrapped in red cellophane, and a thermos that is passed around more often than strictly necessary. They are volunteers in the Shorebird Watch program, and their job begins precisely when everyone else's ends.

The birds they protect are easy to overlook. Hooded plovers are small, sandy-coloured, and almost perfectly camouflaged against the shells and dry seaweed where they nest. Rather than building nests in trees, they scrape a shallow hollow directly into the sand and lay two or three speckled eggs. The strategy works well against hawks and gulls, which rarely notice a nest that looks like every other patch of beach. It works badly against almost everything else: bicycles, dogs, four-wheel drives, and the simple human habit of walking in a straight line without looking down.

Ten years ago, the local council counted only four nesting pairs along the whole stretch of coast. The volunteers decided that counting was not the same as helping. They began marking nests with low, unobtrusive fencing and small signs that explained, without scolding, why a patch of sand had suddenly been declared off-limits. They also discovered, after a season of trial and error, that the most effective tool was conversation. A person who has been told about a nest by someone holding a clipboard is far more likely to walk around it than a person who has merely read a notice.

By last summer the count had risen to nineteen pairs. The volunteers are careful not to claim all the credit. Fox control, changes to dog regulations, and a run of unusually mild springs each played a part. Yet the program's coordinator, Meera Rahal, argues that the most durable change was cultural. "People used to see the beach as a place with nothing on it," she says. "Now they arrive expecting to find something worth protecting."

The work is not glamorous. Some nights the wind carries sand into every pocket and the birds fail to appear at all. But the volunteers return the following evening regardless, thermos in hand, because the plovers cannot file a complaint and cannot move their nests when a school holiday begins.

questions.options: To count visitors using the beach each evening|To protect the nests of small birds that breed on the sand|To train volunteers to become professional wildlife rangers|To persuade the council to close the beach to the public
questions.explanation: Volunteers mark nests, talk to beachgoers and protect plover nests laid directly in the sand.

questions.explanation: The camouflage works against gulls and hawks but fails against bicycles, dogs, four-wheel drives and careless walkers.

questions.options: Building tall fences around each nest|Reporting careless visitors to the council|Talking directly with people about the nests|Handing out printed notices along the beach
questions.explanation: The passage states that 'the most effective tool was conversation', contrasting it with merely reading a notice.

questions.options: A permanent increase in council funding for the beach|A shift in how people think about the beach and its wildlife|A change in the regulations controlling dog ownership|A long-term rise in the number of volunteers joining
questions.explanation: 'Cultural' refers to attitudes: visitors now expect to find something worth protecting.

questions.options: To suggest that the volunteers' work was unlikely to have mattered|To show the increase was real but partly caused by conditions outside the program|To argue that fox control was the true cause of the increase|To criticise the council for taking credit for the volunteers' efforts
questions.explanation: The passage acknowledges fox control, dog regulations and mild springs, indicating multiple causes.

questions.options: Amusement at their own stubbornness|Frustration with the council's slow response|Duty, because the birds depend entirely on them|Doubt about whether the program is worth continuing
questions.explanation: The birds cannot complain or relocate, which explains why volunteers keep returning.

title: Original: The Sound of the Warning
passage:
The Sound of the Warning

Tessa had worked in her family's boat shed for three summers, long enough to know that the harbour had its own vocabulary. A certain slap of rope against a mast meant nothing. A particular creak of the tin roof meant rain by evening. But the low, flat note of the warning buoy beyond the breakwater, sounding twice and then stopping, meant that the weather had changed its mind about being reasonable.

That afternoon the buoy spoke twice, and Tessa stopped sanding.

Her father was inland, collecting a trailer of timber, and would not be back until dark. The shed radio muttered about a front moving up the coast faster than forecast. Tessa walked to the end of the jetty and counted the boats still in the water. Eleven. Most were owned by people who checked forecasts the way other people checked football scores, but one belonged to old Mr Kowalski, who had rowed out at dawn and had not come back.

She found him at the far end of the moorings, wrestling with a tarpaulin that the wind kept taking from him like a joke it had not tired of. He was seventy-eight, and his hands worked faster than his shoulders could follow. Tessa did not ask whether he wanted help. She simply took the far corner of the tarpaulin and held it, and after a moment he stopped arguing with the sky and started tying knots with her.

They worked without much conversation. When the boat was covered, he stood with his back to the wind and looked at the water for a while. "I heard it too," he said at last. "I told myself I had time."

"Everyone tells themselves that," Tessa said, and then wondered whether it had sounded rude. He laughed, which she had not expected, and said that her grandmother had once said exactly the same thing in exactly the same tone.

By the time the front arrived, the last of the eleven boats was tied down and the jetty lamps were swaying. Tessa went back to the shed, hung her wet jacket on the same hook her father used, and wrote two words on the whiteboard where the day's jobs were listed: BUOY TWICE.

Her father read it when he came home and did not ask what it meant. He only nodded, and added it to the list of things the shed would now watch for, the way the family had been watching the same stretch of water for three generations.

questions.explanation: The opening paragraph explains that the buoy sounding twice means the weather has changed.

questions.explanation: The metaphor presents harbour sounds as a language she has learned to interpret.

questions.explanation: She acts directly rather than questioning him, showing tact as well as concern.

questions.explanation: The line implies he heard the warning but assumed he had enough time.

questions.options: Shows he is mocking her inexperience|Suggests the two characters share a connection across generations|Proves that the storm has passed safely|Indicates that he has forgotten the danger
questions.explanation: He says her grandmother used the same words in the same tone, linking the past and present.

questions.options: They distrust Tessa's judgement and check her work|They value knowledge that is passed on and learnt from experience|They believe written instructions are more reliable than observation|They treat the danger of storms as an unavoidable part of work
questions.explanation: He simply nods and adds it to the family's ongoing record of what to watch for.

title: Original: Extract A & B — Phones at School
passage:
Extract A: The Case for the Locked Cupboard

When our local high school banned phones during class hours, the complaints arrived faster than the results. Parents worried about emergencies; students worried about boredom. Two terms later, the change is the most popular thing the school has done in years, and it is not because the students have suddenly fallen in love with silence.

Before the ban, a typical lesson was interrupted by an average of nine notifications per student, most of them trivial. Teachers reported that the hardest part of their job was not explaining algebra but competing with a screen for attention. The school's decision to require phones to be locked in a cupboard until the final bell was not an act of fear. It was an admission that willpower is a poor defence against a device engineered by thousands of highly paid adults to be irresistible.

Critics say students must learn to manage distractions, since the adult world is full of them. That argument is attractive until you notice that the adult world also has the right to leave the room, close a tab, or set a boundary. A classroom is not a workplace. It is a place where attention is the raw material of learning. Asking a thirteen-year-old to defend that attention alone is not toughness; it is negligence dressed up as character building.

Extract B: A Teacher's Reluctant Reversal

I argued against a phone ban for six years, and I was wrong, though not for the reasons the ban's supporters give. My objection was practical: the devices are the cheapest research library a school will ever own. In my geography class, students photograph fieldwork sites, check rainfall records in real time, and compare news reports from three countries before the first bell.

What changed my mind was not the distraction statistics but the pattern of who was affected. The students who lost the most when phones were permitted were not the ones scrolling openly. They were the quiet, conscientious students who felt obliged to answer every message so that nobody would think they were ignoring them. A rule removes the need for that decision, and for the social cost of making it.

I still resist the language of purity that surrounds this debate. Phones are not cigarettes and screens are not poison. When a class needs a live weather radar, we should be allowed to use one. But a rule that is clear, consistent and reviewed each year is not an attack on technology. It is an acknowledgement that the classroom is the only place where a student should be able to expect that attention is protected.

questions.stem: What do both extracts agree about?
questions.options: Phones should be banned permanently in every school|Students' attention in class is worth protecting|Teachers should confiscate phones without any rules|Technology has no place in a geography classroom
questions.explanation: Extract A calls attention 'the raw material of learning'; Extract B wants students to expect their attention to be protected.

questions.stem: Extract A describes the ban as 'an admission' because the school accepted that:
questions.options: Parents had been complaining for several terms|Willpower alone is not a fair defence against deliberately engaging devices|Teachers were unable to plan lessons effectively|Students preferred cupboards to classrooms
questions.explanation: The writer argues devices are engineered to be irresistible, so relying on willpower is unrealistic.

questions.stem: In Extract A, the phrase 'negligence dressed up as character building' is used to criticise:
questions.options: Teachers who refuse to use technology in lessons|The claim that students should handle distraction unaided|Parents who buy their children expensive phones|Schools that review their rules every year
questions.explanation: The writer rejects the argument that managing distraction alone proves toughness.

questions.stem: Why was the writer of Extract B originally opposed to a ban?
questions.options: Because phones provide cheap and immediate access to research tools|Because the school could not afford cupboards for the devices|Because the distraction statistics had not yet been published|Because students threatened to protest against the rule
questions.explanation: Extract B calls phones 'the cheapest research library a school will ever own'.

questions.stem: What surprised the writer of Extract B about the effects of allowing phones?
questions.options: That the loudest students were the least affected|That quiet, conscientious students carried the greatest social cost|That geography results improved sharply|That teachers used phones more than students did
questions.explanation: The writer notes the quiet students felt obliged to answer every message to avoid seeming rude.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the difference in tone between the two extracts?
questions.options: Extract A is firm and argumentative; Extract B is reflective and self-critical|Extract A is humorous; Extract B is sarcastic|Both extracts are neutral reports of research findings|Extract A is uncertain; Extract B is aggressive
questions.explanation: Extract A argues strongly against critics, while Extract B admits 'I was wrong' and reflects on why.

title: Original: The Quiet Work of Mangroves
passage:
The Quiet Work of Mangroves

Most coastal visitors walk past a mangrove forest without noticing it. There is nothing to photograph that announces itself: no waterfall, no cliff, no bright birds arranged conveniently on a branch. The trees stand in shallow, muddy water on stilt-like roots, and the smell is not pleasant. Yet the tangle that looks like neglect is one of the most productive structures on the Australian coastline.

The first thing a mangrove does is stand still. Its roots slow the movement of water, and slowed water drops the fine sediment it is carrying. Over years, this quiet settling builds new land where there was once open channel. The same roots absorb the energy of waves that would otherwise reach the shore, which is why coastal engineers now study mangroves as an alternative to concrete walls. A sea wall protects exactly the stretch of coast behind it. A mangrove forest protects everything it touches, and it repairs itself after storms.

Below the surface the work continues. The root system is a nursery. Juvenile fish, prawns and crabs shelter among the roots, where larger predators cannot easily follow. When those animals mature, many of them move into open water, which means that a mangrove forest supports fisheries far from the forest itself. People who have never seen a mangrove still depend on what it shelters.

The trees also store carbon in a way that is difficult to match. Because waterlogged mud contains very little oxygen, dead leaves and roots break down extremely slowly. Carbon that would be released within a year or two in a dry forest can remain locked in mangrove sediment for centuries. When a mangrove is cleared for a marina or a car park, that buried carbon is exposed, and the loss is much larger than the loss of the trees themselves.

This is why restoration projects are so frustrating and so valuable. A mangrove can be ripped out in an afternoon, but a new forest takes decades to establish, and only if the hydrology, the mud and the tides are right. The volunteers who plant seedlings in knee-deep silt will not see a mature forest in their lifetimes.

It is worth remembering the next time a coastal path passes a stand of grey-green trees with their feet in the water. What looks like a swamp is doing several jobs at once, without being asked, and it has been doing them longer than any seawall on the coast.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
questions.options: Mangrove forests are attractive but difficult to photograph|Mangrove forests perform several valuable functions that are easily overlooked|Coastal engineers prefer concrete walls to natural defences|Mangrove forests should be cleared to create new land
questions.explanation: The passage argues that what looks like a swamp is doing several jobs at once, unnoticed.

questions.stem: How do mangrove roots create new land?
questions.options: By growing upwards until they break the surface of the water|By slowing water so that it drops the sediment it carries|By trapping fish that decay and enrich the soil|By absorbing salt from the surrounding mud
questions.explanation: Slowed water releases fine sediment, which gradually settles and builds new ground.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare a sea wall with a mangrove forest?
questions.options: To show that sea walls cost more to build|To highlight that mangroves protect a wider area and repair themselves|To argue that sea walls should be removed from all coasts|To explain how engineers measure wave energy
questions.explanation: The text contrasts a wall protecting one stretch with a forest protecting everything it touches and self-repairing.

questions.stem: The phrase 'the root system is a nursery' means that the roots:
questions.options: Provide shelter where young sea creatures can grow safely|Are used to grow seedlings for restoration projects|Look after plants that have been damaged by storms|Supply food directly to adult prawns and crabs
questions.explanation: 'Nursery' indicates a protected place where juveniles shelter from predators.

questions.stem: Why does clearing a mangrove release more carbon than simply removing trees?
questions.options: The trees are much larger than ordinary forest trees|The sediment stores carbon that has built up over centuries|Mangroves absorb carbon from the sea as well as the air|Machinery used for clearing produces extra emissions
questions.explanation: Waterlogged mud slows decay, so carbon stays locked in sediment for centuries until it is exposed.

questions.stem: The tone of the final paragraph can best be described as:
questions.options: Angry and accusatory|Quietly appreciative and persuasive|Amused and light-hearted|Uncertain and questioning
questions.explanation: The ending invites the reader to respect the unseen work of mangroves rather than attacking anyone.

title: Original: The Map That Was Wrong
passage:
The Map That Was Wrong

In the winter of 1887, a fourteen-year-old named Alice Brennan was employed to copy maps in the survey office at Port Wren, a job she had won because her handwriting was neat and her wages could be small. Her desk stood beside a window that looked onto the yard where the horses were kept, and her task each morning was to reproduce, in ink, the pencil drawings that the surveyors brought back from the interior.

For three months she copied without complaint. Then, on a Tuesday, she noticed something that would not let her sleep. Two maps of the same district, drawn eighteen months apart, disagreed about a creek. On the older map the creek ran east and joined the river above the ford. On the newer one it simply stopped, as though the water had changed its mind. The newer map was signed by Mr Ellery, the senior surveyor, who did not enjoy being corrected.

Alice checked the field notebooks, which she was not strictly permitted to read. There, in pencil, was the answer: the creek did run east. The surveyor had written that the crossing was impassable after rain. On the finished map the creek had been copied incorrectly, and the note about the crossing had been omitted altogether.

She told her supervisor, who told her that maps were not the business of copyists. She told him again the following week, with the notebook open on his desk, and was sent home without pay for impertinence. It would have ended there, except that the incorrect map had already been sent to the roads office, where it was being used to plan a bridge.

The bridge was built the following summer, four hundred metres downstream of the only place where the banks were firm enough to hold it. It lasted two seasons. When the enquiry was held, Mr Ellery explained that the drawing had been copied in a hurry. Alice, who was by then fifteen and earning slightly more, was asked why she had not reported the error sooner. She said that she had, twice, and that the second time had cost her a week's wages. The room was quiet for a moment. The enquiry recommended that field notebooks be checked against finished maps before they left the office, and that copyists be permitted to raise questions about the documents they handled.

Alice stayed at the survey office for another nine years. She never became a surveyor; that door was closed to her for reasons nobody thought to examine. But the rule she was indirectly responsible for outlived every map she copied, and in later years the clerks who followed it had no idea whose stubbornness had put it there.

questions.options: Because she had trained as a surveyor in the city|Because her handwriting was neat and her wages could be low|Because her family owned the land being surveyed|Because she could read the field notebooks quickly
questions.explanation: The first paragraph states both reasons directly.

questions.stem: What exactly was wrong with the newer map?

questions.explanation: The passage explains the creek was copied incorrectly and the note about the impassable crossing was omitted.

questions.stem: The phrase 'maps were not the business of copyists' is used to show that her supervisor:
questions.options: Believed accuracy was everyone's responsibility|Rejected her concern because of her low position|Wanted her to become a surveyor herself|Had already noticed the error himself
questions.explanation: The remark dismisses her right to raise the issue because of her role, not because the error was unimportant.

questions.stem: What finally forced the error into the open?
questions.options: A clerk in the roads office checked the map against the notebook|The bridge failed and an enquiry was held|Mr Ellery reported the mistake himself|Alice published a letter in the local paper
questions.explanation: The incorrectly sited bridge lasted two seasons, leading to an enquiry.

questions.stem: Why does the author include Alice's comment that reporting the error had cost her a week's wages?
questions.options: To show that she expected compensation|To reveal how she had been treated for doing the right thing|To suggest she was exaggerating the punishment|To explain why she later left the office
questions.explanation: Her statement demonstrates the cost of her honesty and silences the room.

questions.options: The maps she copied with unusual neatness|A procedure that outlived her and protected later work|Her promotion to a better-paid position|Her testimony at the enquiry
questions.explanation: The rule she was indirectly responsible for outlived every map she copied.

title: Original: Afternoon Train
passage:
Afternoon Train

The platform holds its breath, then lets it go -
a whistle splits the heat in two, and we
are moving, sliding past the ticket booth,
past sunburnt fences leaning into shade.

The paddocks open like a held-out hand:
white cockatoos lift off a single wire
and scatter into commas on the sky.
A creek appears, considers us, moves on.

Between the stations someone's radio
plays half a song, then loses it to static,
and two old men discuss a football match
as though the score could settle something else.

At Wattle Creek the light turns soft and low,
my reflection floats beside me in the glass,
half traveller, half ghost who cannot leave,
and the long grass bows, and bows, and lets us pass.

questions.explanation: The simile emphasises how the birds look from the moving train - small marks spread across the sky.

questions.explanation: The creek seems to pause and then continue, implying a world that exists beyond the train.

questions.explanation: Looking at a reflection while moving creates a sense of being both present and apart from the scene.

title: Original: How Bees Find Their Way
passage:
How Bees Find Their Way

A honeybee leaving a hive to search for flowers is doing something that looks, at first, impossible. It may fly five kilometres in a wandering line, visit several patches of blossoms, and then return to a hive the size of a shoebox without hesitation. The bee has no map, no landmarks drawn for its benefit, and no way to ask for directions. What it has instead is a set of overlapping methods, each fairly crude on its own, which together amount to an extraordinarily reliable navigation system.

The first method is memory of movement. As the bee flies, it keeps a running tally of direction and distance by watching the world slide past its eyes. This process is imperfect and accumulates error over long flights, which is why bees leaving a new food source often loop back to look at it before heading home. The loop gives them a clearer record of the route.

Near the hive, sight takes over. Bees learn the arrangement of trees, fences, sheds and hedges around their home and use these shapes as a sequence of markers, much as a driver uses a series of familiar buildings. Researchers who moved a hive a short distance found that returning foragers hovered at the old site in confusion, then searched outwards along the ring of landmarks they remembered.

The final method is the oddest. Bees can detect the polarisation pattern of sunlight, a property of light invisible to humans, and use it to find the position of the sun even when the sky is heavily overcast. Because the hive's dances communicate direction relative to the sun, this ability means a bee can interpret those instructions on a cloudy afternoon when no sun is visible at all.

What all three methods share is that none of them is accurate on its own. Memory drifts. Landmarks disappear. Clouds thicken. The system works because the bee does not rely on any single source but keeps correcting one against another. Engineers who build navigation systems for robots have taken an interest for exactly this reason: combining several noisy signals produces a result that is steadier than any one of them.

questions.options: Bees navigate using several imperfect methods that correct one another|Bees can see landmarks that are invisible to humans|Bees travel further than scientists previously believed|Robots have copied the bee's navigation system exactly
questions.explanation: The passage stresses that no single method is accurate, but together they are reliable.

questions.stem: Why do bees sometimes loop back to look at a new food source before returning home?
questions.options: To check whether the flowers have been visited by other bees|To build a clearer memory of the route back|To warn other insects away from the flowers|To collect more pollen before flying to the hive
questions.explanation: The loop gives them a clearer record of the route, compensating for drifting memory.

questions.explanation: Foragers hovered at the old site, then searched outwards along the familiar ring of landmarks.

questions.stem: Why is the ability to detect polarised light useful to a bee?
questions.options: It allows the bee to see flowers in dark conditions|It reveals the sun's position even when the sky is overcast|It helps the bee measure the distance to the hive|It warns the bee when a storm is approaching
questions.explanation: The passage states this lets bees interpret dance instructions on cloudy afternoons.

questions.options: Bees communicating loudly inside the hive|Mixing imperfect information sources to produce a steadier result|Robot sensors that malfunction in cloudy weather|Researchers recording bees with several microphones
questions.explanation: 'Noisy' here means imprecise or error-prone, not literally loud.

questions.options: To suggest that scientists should stop studying insects|To show that the bee's method has practical value beyond biology|To argue that robots are better navigators than bees|To explain how the hive experiment was conducted
questions.explanation: The comparison links the bee's combined-signal strategy to real engineering practice.

title: Original: The Real Price of a Cheap T-shirt
passage:
The Real Price of a Cheap T-shirt

A t-shirt that costs nine dollars is not cheap. It is simply priced in a way that hides most of its cost from the person paying at the counter.

Consider what happens before the shirt reaches a shop. A crop must be grown, usually cotton, which in many regions requires enormous volumes of water and frequent applications of pesticide. The fibre is then spun, dyed, cut and sewn, often across several countries, before being shipped thousands of kilometres. Every one of these steps consumes resources and produces waste, and none of that vanishes because the label says nine dollars. It has merely been charged to somebody else: to a river downstream of a dye house, to a farmer breathing pesticide, or to a worker paid by the piece rather than by the hour.

Supporters of the current system argue that inexpensive clothing has been a genuine benefit. It is true that a family on a tight budget is better off when school uniforms and children's clothes cost less. But this argument confuses low price with low cost. A shirt that loses its shape after eight washes is not cheaper than one that lasts four years; it is a more expensive shirt purchased repeatedly. The household budget eventually pays for the difference, with interest.

The environmental arithmetic is just as unfavourable. Clothing that fails quickly becomes waste quickly. In many countries, a large share of discarded textiles ends up buried or burned rather than recycled, and the fibres that do get recycled are frequently of lower quality. Meanwhile, the pressure to release new collections every few weeks means that design decisions are made for the photograph rather than for the fifth year of wear.

What would a better system look like? Not a return to a world where clothing was scarce and expensive for everyone, which is a fantasy that helps nobody. A better system would make durability visible: clear labelling of how many washes a garment survived in testing, repair services that are cheaper than replacement, and tax rules that reward mending over discarding. None of these ideas is glamorous. All of them attack the same problem from different sides, which is that the price on the tag and the cost to the world have drifted far apart.

The next time a shirt seems like a bargain, the honest question is not whether you can afford it. It is what the difference is being paid for, and by whom.

questions.stem: What is the writer's central argument?
questions.options: Clothing should be manufactured only in one country|Low prices hide costs that are paid by other people and the environment|Cotton farming should be banned completely|Families on tight budgets buy too many clothes
questions.explanation: The essay argues that a low tag price conceals costs shifted onto workers, communities and ecosystems.

questions.stem: The writer says the counter-argument 'confuses low price with low cost' because:
questions.options: Cheap clothing is usually better made than expensive clothing|Garments that wear out quickly must be replaced, so the saving disappears|Families who buy cheap clothes do not care about quality|Retailers set prices without considering production costs
questions.explanation: The writer explains that a shirt failing after eight washes is a more expensive shirt bought repeatedly.

questions.stem: The tone of the third paragraph can best be described as:
questions.options: Hostile towards families on tight budgets|Fair-minded, conceding a point before rejecting it|Amused by the arguments of supporters|Uncertain about whether cheap clothing helps anyone
questions.explanation: The writer accepts that inexpensive clothing can help some households, then challenges the conclusion drawn from it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the writer's suggested improvements?

title: Original: Cloze — The Bridge at Kestrel Creek
passage:
The Bridge at Kestrel Creek

For thirty years the bridge at Kestrel Creek carried almost nothing: a farmer's ute, a postman on Tuesdays, and the occasional cyclist who had (1) ______ the turn-off and was too proud to ask for directions. Then the highway was closed for repairs, and within a week the old bridge became the busiest road in the district.

The council had always (2) ______ the bridge as a liability. Its timber deck had been patched so many times that no two planks matched, and the (3) ______ railing leaned like a fence after a storm. Engineers had inspected it twice and delivered the same verdict both times: sound, but only just.

What the engineers could not measure was the bridge's hold on the people who used it. Drivers slowed instinctively at the first plank, not because they had been told to, but because everyone did. Strangers (4) ______ hands as they passed, a habit nobody could explain and nobody wanted to break.

When the highway reopened, the traffic (5) ______ back to almost nothing. A reporter came out to write a gentle piece about the bridge's brief fame, and discovered that the council had already (6) ______ a demolition date. The story changed the plan. Instead of a new concrete crossing, the council agreed to replace the deck plank by plank, (7) ______ the original shape of the structure.

The work took eighteen months and cost more than the demolition would have. The bridge is now listed on the local heritage register, which means it is protected and, more importantly, (8) ______ to the people who keep using it out of habit rather than necessity.
